errors: No mathematical content, so no mathematical errors. As a copy of Locke the excerpt is substantially faithful to the standard text of Essay II.xxi §§46-47 and §71; only minor orthographic and capitalisation differences appear (e.g. 'judg'd', 'call'd', capitalised nouns, which are typical of 18th-century editions).
The parenthesised '(Uneasiness)' in the copy is not in Locke's printed text, which reads 'the greatest and most pressing uneasiness'. The brackets or underlining are the copyist's emphasis.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a reading-note copy of a well-known passage of Locke on free will, with no mathematics and no original contribution. Riemann's philosophical reading (Herbart, psychology, the will) is already documented in his Nachlass, so a Locke excerpt is unremarkable.
transcription_corrections: The circled '(60)' at the right end of line 9 is the archival folio number written on the page, not part of the text.
Fragments in the far left margin ('upf', 'ully' or similar) are bleed or edge text from the facing leaf and should not be transcribed as part of this page.
'(Uneasiness)' appears in the manuscript set off by parentheses or brackets; this is the copyist's emphasis, not Locke's punctuation.

The section headings 'The greatest good, not being desired, moves not the will', 'Due consideration raises Desire' and 'The Power to suspend the Prosecution of any Desire, makes Way for Consideration' are Locke's marginal summaries (§45, §46, §47), set within German-style low/high quotation marks („ ").
